questions.question: An object moves at constant speed v around a circle of radius r. Using a vector diagram of the velocities at two positions A and B, derive an expression for its acceleration.
questions.answer: a = v^2 / r, directed towards the centre of the circle.
steps: Velocity is a vector tangent to the circle; at A and B it has the same magnitude v but a different direction.
Draw vA and vB from a common origin; the change in velocity dv = vB - vA points towards the centre.
For a small angle theta between A and B, the velocity triangle is isosceles and dv is approximately v x theta.
The arc length r x theta = v x dt, so theta = v dt / r.
Acceleration a = dv / dt = (v x v dt / r) / dt = v^2 / r, directed to the centre.

questions.question: Complete a free body force diagram for one aeroplane on its wire at the given speed, where the wire is at 19 degrees to the vertical.
questions.answer: Two forces: weight mg acting vertically downwards, and tension T along the wire, directed up towards the point of support at 19 degrees to the vertical.
steps: Draw the weight W = mg as an arrow vertically downwards from the dot (the aeroplane).
Draw the tension T in the wire as an arrow along the wire, pointing up and inwards towards the support, at 19 degrees to the vertical.
These are the only two forces (the horizontal component of T is the resultant force that provides the centripetal force).

questions.question: Aeroplanes on wires at 19 degrees to the vertical follow a circle of diameter 10.8 cm. Mass of each aeroplane is 5.2 g. Show that 4 complete rotations take about 3 s.
questions.answer: One rotation takes 0.79 s, so 4 rotations take about 3.2 s (about 3 s).
steps: Radius of the circular path r = 10.8 cm / 2 = 0.054 m.
Vertically T cos(19) = mg; horizontally T sin(19) = m omega^2 r (centripetal force).
Dividing the two equations gives tan(19) = omega^2 r / g, so omega^2 = g tan(19) / r.
omega^2 = 9.81 x 0.3443 / 0.054 = 62.5, so omega = 7.91 rad s^-1 (mass cancels).
Period for one rotation T = 2 pi / omega = 0.794 s.
Four rotations take 4 x 0.794 = 3.2 s, which is about 3 s.

questions.question: The canopy radius is increased and the platform rotates at the same angular velocity. Student A says the wires could become vertical; Student B says the wires would be at more than 19 degrees to the vertical. Explain which student, if either, is correct.
questions.answer: Student B is correct: tan(theta) = omega^2 r / g increases with r, so the angle exceeds 19 degrees; a vertical wire would need r = 0, so Student A is wrong.
steps: From part (ii), for steady circular motion tan(theta) = omega^2 r / g.
The angular velocity is unchanged and g is constant, so tan(theta) is proportional to the radius r.
A larger radius gives a larger tan(theta), so the wires tilt further from the vertical.
Wires are vertical only when tan(theta) = 0, which needs r = 0, but the circle is then not formed while omega is non-zero.
Student A is incorrect and Student B is correct: the angle is greater than 19 degrees.

questions.question: A turntable rotates at 33 revolutions per minute. Select the angular velocity in rad s^-1 from the options.
steps: 33 revolutions per minute = 33 / 60 revolutions per second.
Each revolution is 2 pi radians, so omega = (33 / 60) x 2 pi = 3.5 rad s^-1, which is option C.

questions.question: A 185 kg go-kart and driver travels at 9.72 m/s round a semicircular end of diameter 30.0 m on a horizontal track. Maximum friction is 1180 N. Show that the design meets the criterion of safe speed up to 35 km/h.
questions.answer: Required centripetal force is 1165 N, which is less than the maximum friction of 1180 N, so the design meets the criteria.
steps: Radius of the semicircular end r = 30.0 m / 2 = 15.0 m.
Friction provides the centripetal force: F = m v^2 / r.
The maximum available friction is 1180 N, which is greater than 1165 N.
The go-kart can take the bend at 9.72 m/s without slipping, so the design meets the criteria.

questions.question: On the banked semicircular end, the go-kart needs no frictional force perpendicular to its motion at speed v. Show that tan(theta) = 2v^2 / (g d), where d is the diameter AB of the curved track. (The formula is not fully reproduced in the text extraction.)
questions.answer: tan(theta) = v^2 / (r g) = 2 v^2 / (g d), where d is the diameter AB.
steps: With no sideways friction, the only forces are weight mg and the normal reaction R.
Vertically R cos(theta) = mg, since there is no vertical acceleration.
Horizontally, towards the centre, R sin(theta) = m v^2 / r.
Dividing the two equations gives tan(theta) = v^2 / (r g).
The radius is r = d / 2, so tan(theta) = 2 v^2 / (g d).

questions.question: Using the design speed of 9.72 m/s and diameter AB = 30.0 m, calculate the banking angle theta for the banked track.
questions.answer: theta = 33 degrees (about 32.7 degrees).
steps: Use tan(theta) = 2 v^2 / (g d).
theta = arctan(0.642) = 32.7 degrees, which is about 33 degrees.

questions.question: A go-kart track has semicircular ends of diameter 30.0 m. The go-kart and driver have mass 185 kg and must travel safely at up to 9.72 m s^-1 on the bends. On a horizontal track the maximum frictional force is 1180 N. A banked track will cost more to build. Suggest whether there are any significant advantages that would justify the cost.
questions.answer: Yes: on the flat track the friction needed (about 1170 N) is only just below the 1180 N maximum, so there is almost no safety margin. A banked track does not rely on sideways friction, so it stays safe in wet or icy conditions and allows higher speeds, which could justify the cost.
steps: Centripetal force needed on the flat track: F = m v^2 / r = 185 x 9.72^2 / 15.0 = 1170 N.
This is only just below the maximum frictional force of 1180 N, so the flat design meets the criteria with almost no margin.
In wet or icy conditions the friction is reduced, so on the flat track the karts could skid outwards on the bends.
On a banked track the horizontal component of the normal contact force provides the centripetal force, so no sideways friction is needed at the design speed.
So the banked track is safer, allows higher speeds and causes less tyre wear, which are significant advantages that could justify the extra cost.

questions.question: A coin of mass 12 g is in contact with the inside of a washing machine drum of diameter 48 cm. The drum rotates about a horizontal axis at 600 rev/min. Calculate the maximum normal contact force exerted by the drum on the coin.
questions.answer: Maximum normal contact force = 11.5 N, at the lowest point of the drum.
steps: Angular velocity omega = 600 rev/min = 10 rev/s = 2 pi x 10 = 62.8 rad s^-1.
Radius r = 48 cm / 2 = 0.24 m.
The normal force is greatest at the bottom, where it must support the weight as well as provide the centripetal force.
At the bottom N - mg = m omega^2 r, so N = m (g + omega^2 r).

questions.question: Add to the diagram the two forces acting on the bob of a conical pendulum.
questions.answer: Weight mg vertically downwards from the bob, and tension T along the wire towards the support.
steps: Draw the weight mg as an arrow vertically downwards from the bob.
Draw the tension T in the wire as an arrow from the bob along the wire towards the support point, at angle theta to the vertical.

questions.question: Derive the equation for the angular velocity omega of the bob of a conical pendulum with wire length l at angle theta to the vertical.
questions.answer: omega = sqrt(g / (l cos(theta))).
steps: Vertically T cos(theta) = mg, since the bob has no vertical acceleration.
Horizontally T sin(theta) = m omega^2 r, where the radius of the circle is r = l sin(theta).
Dividing gives tan(theta) = omega^2 l sin(theta) / g.
Cancelling sin(theta) gives 1 / cos(theta) = omega^2 l / g.
Therefore omega^2 = g / (l cos(theta)), so omega = sqrt(g / (l cos(theta))).

questions.question: A clock needs a period of 5.0 s. The wire length is 6.4 m and the angle to the vertical is 13.9 degrees. Deduce whether this arrangement gives the required period.
questions.answer: omega = 1.26 rad/s gives T = 5.00 s, so the arrangement does give the required period.
steps: Use omega = sqrt(g / (l cos(theta))).
cos(13.9 degrees) = 0.9707, so l cos(theta) = 6.4 x 0.9707 = 6.21 m.
Period T = 2 pi / omega = 6.283 / 1.257 = 5.00 s.
This equals the required 5.0 s, so the arrangement is suitable.

questions.question: A toy car of mass 33 g is released from 25 cm above point A on a track with a loop. Point C is 22 cm above A. Friction is negligible. Deduce whether the car completes the loop and reaches point D.
questions.answer: No: the car does not complete the loop. At C its speed is 0.77 m s^-1, below the 1.04 m s^-1 needed.
steps: A is the bottom and C the top of the loop, so its diameter is 22 cm and the radius is r = 0.11 m.
To stay on the track at the top the weight must not be more than the centripetal force: m g <= m v^2 / r, so v_min = sqrt(g r) = sqrt(9.81 x 0.11) = 1.04 m s^-1.

Speed at C by conservation of energy (no friction): C is 22 cm above A and the release point is 25 cm above A, so the car has fallen only 3 cm below its starting height: 1/2 v^2 = g (0.25 - 0.22), so v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.030) = 0.77 m s^-1.
0.77 m s^-1 is less than 1.04 m s^-1. At C the centripetal force needed (m v^2 / r = 0.033 x 0.589 / 0.11 = 0.18 N) is less than the weight (0.32 N), so the car loses contact and falls off.
It would need to be released at least 22 + r / 2 = 27.5 cm above A to complete the loop, so it does not reach D.

questions.question: A website claims the Moon's orbital radius increases each year while its period stays constant. Select the correct row of the table, A to D, if the statement is true.
questions.answer: B: angular velocity constant; speed increasing
steps: The period T is constant, so the angular velocity omega = 2 pi / T is constant.
The speed v = omega r. With omega constant and r increasing, the speed increases. This is row B.

questions.question: An aeroplane flies at constant speed v around a horizontal circular path of radius r. Using a vector diagram of its velocities at two positions A and B, derive an expression for its acceleration.
questions.answer: a = v^2 / r, directed towards the centre of the horizontal circle.
steps: Velocity is tangent to the circle, so vA and vB have equal magnitude v and different directions.
The change in velocity dv = vB - vA on the vector diagram points towards the centre.
For a small angle theta between the positions, dv is approximately v x theta.
Arc length r theta = v dt, so theta = v dt / r.
a = dv / dt = v^2 / r, directed to the centre.

questions.question: Explain how banking allows an aeroplane to fly in a horizontal circular path, given that the lift force acts perpendicular to its wings.
questions.answer: The tilted lift has a horizontal component that provides the centripetal force and a vertical component that balances the weight.
steps: When banked, the wings tilt, so the lift acts perpendicular to them, towards the centre of the circle.
The vertical component of lift balances the weight, so the aeroplane keeps its height.
The horizontal component of lift points towards the centre and provides the centripetal force.
Without banking, lift is vertical and nothing points towards the centre, so the aeroplane cannot turn.
Banking therefore lets the aeroplane turn in a horizontal circle at constant height.

questions.question: During banking the wings are at 5.2 degrees to the horizontal. The aeroplane (mass 4.1 x 10^5 kg) flies at a constant 530 m/s. Calculate the radius of the circular path.
questions.answer: Radius = 3.1 x 10^5 m (about 310 km).
steps: The lift is perpendicular to the wings, so it makes 5.2 degrees with the vertical.
Vertically L cos(5.2) = mg; horizontally L sin(5.2) = m v^2 / r.
Dividing gives tan(5.2) = v^2 / (r g), so r = v^2 / (g tan(5.2)).
The mass cancels, so the radius is about 3.1 x 10^5 m.

questions.question: A poi ball moves clockwise in a circle of radius r with constant speed v. Using a vector diagram of its velocities at two positions A and B, derive the equation for its centripetal acceleration.
questions.answer: a = v^2 / r, directed towards the centre O.
steps: Velocities at A and B are tangent to the circle and have equal magnitude v.
The vector change dv = vB - vA on the diagram points towards the centre O.
For a small angle theta, dv is approximately v theta, and the arc gives theta = v dt / r.
a = dv / dt = v^2 / r, directed to the centre.

questions.question: The poi ball completes 1.3 revolutions per second on a circle of radius 0.58 m. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.answer: a = 38.7 m s^-2 (about 39 m s^-2), directed towards the centre.
steps: Angular velocity omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 1.3 = 8.17 rad s^-1.
Centripetal acceleration a = omega^2 r.

questions.question: The child says that as the poi ball moves round the circle at constant speed, the size of the force on his hand changes. Discuss whether this comment is correct.
questions.answer: Correct: the speed is constant but the tension changes with position because weight adds to or subtracts from the centripetal force.
steps: Constant speed means the resultant force towards the centre is always m v^2 / r.
The tension is the resultant towards the centre plus or minus the weight component along the radius.
At the top the weight acts towards the centre: T + mg = m v^2 / r, so T = m v^2 / r - mg (smallest).
At the bottom the weight acts away from the centre: T - mg = m v^2 / r, so T = m v^2 / r + mg (largest).
The force on the hand therefore changes with position, so the child's comment is correct.

questions.question: Draw the free-body force diagram for the sphere of the hammer at the position shown, where the chain is at 40 degrees to the horizontal.
questions.answer: Two forces on the sphere: weight mg vertically downwards, and tension T along the chain towards the thrower (down and inwards at 40 degrees below the horizontal).
steps: Draw the weight mg as an arrow vertically downwards from the dot.
Draw the tension T along the chain, pointing from the sphere towards the thrower's hands, i.e. down and to the left at 40 degrees below the horizontal.
Label both arrows. (There is no centripetal force arrow; it is the resultant of these two.)

questions.question: Explain why the sphere of the hammer moves in a circle.
questions.answer: The horizontal component of the chain tension acts towards the centre of the circle as a resultant centripetal force, perpendicular to the velocity.
steps: The chain is taut, so the tension acts along the chain towards the athlete's hands.
The tension has a horizontal component pointing towards the centre of the circle.
The vertical component of tension balances the weight of the sphere.
This horizontal resultant is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes direction but not speed.
The sphere therefore continues to move in a circle.

questions.question: The sphere completes 2.8 revolutions per second at a distance of 1.5 m from the centre of the circle. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.answer: Acceleration = 464 m s^-2 (about 4.6 x 10^2 m s^-2), towards the centre.
steps: Angular velocity omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 2.8 = 17.6 rad s^-1.
Centripetal acceleration a = omega^2 r = 309.5 x 1.5 = 464 m s^-2.
The acceleration is directed towards the centre of the circle.

questions.question: The sphere is released at 28 m/s at 40 degrees to the horizontal, from a height of 1.5 m above the ground. The women's Olympic record is 83 m. Deduce whether this throw would break the record, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: Range is about 80 m (80.5 m), which is less than 83 m, so the throw would not break the record.
steps: Horizontal velocity u_x = 28 cos(40) = 21.4 m s^-1, which stays constant without air resistance.
Vertical velocity u_y = 28 sin(40) = 18.0 m s^-1 upwards.
Taking upwards as positive: -1.5 = 18.0 t - 4.91 t^2.
Solve 4.91 t^2 - 18.0 t - 1.5 = 0; the positive root is t = 3.75 s.
Horizontal range = 21.4 x 3.75 = 80.5 m.
80.5 m is less than 83 m, so the throw would not break the record.

questions.question: The heel of a hockey stick moves horizontally in a circle of radius 0.80 m, turning through 1.3 rad in 0.22 s. Calculate its speed.
questions.answer: Speed of heel = 4.7 m s^-1.
steps: Angular velocity omega = angle / time = 1.3 / 0.22 = 5.91 rad s^-1.
Linear speed v = omega r.
The speed of the heel is about 4.7 m s^-1.

questions.question: Using the scaled vector diagram of the heel momentum (3.0 N s) and the ball's momentum (ball mass 160 g, speed 13 m/s before and 16 m/s after), deduce whether momentum is conserved.
questions.answer: Yes: the vector sum of the initial momenta is about 2.5 N s, which equals the ball's final momentum of 2.56 N s within the accuracy of the data.
steps: Ball momentum before: 0.160 x 13 = 2.08 N s (towards the heel). Ball momentum after: 0.160 x 16 = 2.56 N s. The heel stops, so it has no momentum afterwards.
Before the collision draw p_heel = 3.0 N s upwards (to scale), then from its tip draw the ball momentum 2.08 N s at 56 degrees to the vertical, in the direction of the ball travel.
The resultant (start of p_heel to end of the ball vector) measures about 2.5 N s, at about 43 degrees to the vertical, up and to the left.
Calculation check: horizontal = 2.08 sin56 = 1.72 N s; vertical = 3.0 - 2.08 cos56 = 1.84 N s; resultant = 2.52 N s.
This matches the ball's final momentum of 2.56 N s in size and direction (within about 2%), so momentum is conserved.

questions.question: The heel has momentum 3.0 N s and speed 5.0 m/s before the collision, and it stops. The ball (160 g) has speeds of 13 m/s before and 16 m/s after. Deduce whether the collision is elastic.
questions.answer: Not elastic: kinetic energy before is about 21.0 J and after about 20.5 J, so kinetic energy is lost.
steps: Mass of heel m = p / v = 3.0 / 5.0 = 0.60 kg.
KE of heel before = 0.5 x 0.60 x 5.0^2 = 7.5 J.
KE of ball before = 0.5 x 0.160 x 13^2 = 13.5 J.
Total KE before = 7.5 + 13.5 = 21.0 J.
After the collision the heel stops, so KE after = 0.5 x 0.160 x 16^2 = 20.5 J.
KE after is less than KE before, so kinetic energy is not conserved and the collision is inelastic.

questions.question: A roundabout makes 2 complete rotations in 12 s. A child stands 1.8 m from the centre. Calculate the speed of the child.
questions.answer: Speed of child = 1.9 m s^-1.
steps: Period T = 12 s / 2 rotations = 6.0 s per rotation.
Angular velocity omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi / 6.0 = 1.047 rad s^-1.
Speed v = omega r = 1.047 x 1.8 = 1.88 m s^-1.
The speed of the child is about 1.9 m s^-1.

questions.question: An aeroplane of mass 1200 kg flies at 54 m/s in a horizontal circle while banked at 20 degrees to the horizontal. Show that the radius of the circular path is about 800 m.
questions.answer: r = v^2 / (g tan(20)) = 817 m, which is about 800 m.
steps: The lift acts perpendicular to the wings, at 20 degrees to the vertical.
Vertically L cos(20) = mg; horizontally L sin(20) = m v^2 / r.
Dividing gives tan(20) = v^2 / (r g), so r = v^2 / (g tan(20)).

questions.question: The aeroplane flies at 54 m/s along the circular path. Determine the time taken to move through 90 degrees of the circle.
questions.answer: Time = 24 s (about 23.8 s).
steps: Arc length for 90 degrees = (pi / 2) r = 1.571 x 817 = 1283 m.
Time t = arc length / speed = 1283 / 54 = 23.8 s.
Equivalently omega = v / r = 0.0661 rad s^-1 and t = (pi / 2) / omega = 23.8 s.
The time is about 24 s.

questions.question: The wings are levelled so the lift is vertical, with the same speed and lift magnitude as before. Explain what happens to the vertical motion of the aeroplane.
questions.answer: The lift is now larger than the weight, so the aeroplane accelerates vertically upwards (climbs).
steps: Originally the vertical component of lift balanced the weight: L cos(20) = mg.
With the wings level, the whole lift L acts vertically upwards.
Since cos(20) is less than 1, L is greater than mg.
The net vertical force is upwards, so the aeroplane accelerates upwards and climbs.

questions.question: A car of mass m travels at constant speed v over the top of a humpback bridge of radius r. Select the expression for the force from the bridge on the car.
questions.answer: C: m g - m v^2 / r
steps: At the top of the bridge the car moves in a circle with the centre below it, so the resultant force is downwards: m v^2 / r.
Forces: weight m g downwards and the normal force N from the bridge upwards: m g - N = m v^2 / r.
So N = m g - m v^2 / r, option C.

questions.question: A passenger claims that an outward centrifugal force acts on them when the car travels round a circular path at high speed. Assess this claim.
questions.answer: The claim is incorrect: there is no outward force; the passenger's inertia carries them straight on, and an inward force from the car provides the centripetal force.
steps: Centrifugal force is not a real force in a non-rotating (inertial) frame; it only appears when working in the rotating frame of the car.
The passenger tends to continue in a straight line because no inward force acts on them initially (Newton's first law).
The car door or seat exerts an inward (centripetal) force on the passenger, which keeps them moving in the circle.
The passenger is pushed against the door by inertia, not by an outward force, so the claim is incorrect.

questions.question: Using the graph of resultant vertical force against time for the toy car in a plastic ball, show that the angular velocity about the ball's centre is about 40 rad/s.
questions.answer: Period T = 0.16 s, so omega = 2 pi / T = 39 rad s^-1, which is about 40 rad s^-1
steps: The force repeats once per revolution. Read the time between successive peaks on the graph: peaks at about 0.04 s, 0.20 s and 0.36 s.
Two periods = 0.36 - 0.04 = 0.32 s, so T = 0.16 s.
omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi / 0.16 = 39 rad s^-1, which is about 40 rad s^-1.

questions.question: The student recorded 86 mm for the ball. Using the car's mass of 9.5 g and the force data from the graph, deduce whether 86 mm is the radius or the diameter.
questions.answer: 86 mm is the diameter: the radius of the car's path is about 43 mm.
steps: The car moves at constant speed in a vertical circle, so the magnitude of the resultant force is the centripetal force m omega^2 r; its vertical component varies sinusoidally, with maximum equal to the amplitude of the graph, 0.63 N.
43 mm is half of 86 mm, so the measured value of 86 mm must be the diameter of the ball.

questions.question: The force exerted by the ball on the car is greatest at 0.04 s and least at 0.12 s. Discuss the position of the car at these two times, considering the forces on it. No further calculations are needed.
questions.answer: At 0.04 s the car is at the bottom of the ball (greatest force); at 0.12 s it is at the top (least force). The two times are half a period apart, giving a period of about 0.16 s.
steps: The car moves in a vertical circle at constant speed, so the resultant force towards the centre is always m v^2 / r.
At the bottom the ball's force R acts upwards and the weight acts downwards: R - mg = m v^2 / r, so R = m v^2 / r + mg (largest).
At the top both R and the weight act downwards towards the centre: R + mg = m v^2 / r, so R = m v^2 / r - mg (smallest).
The greatest force at 0.04 s means the car is at the bottom, and the least force at 0.12 s means it is at the top.
The bottom and top are half a revolution apart, so half a period is 0.08 s and T is about 0.16 s.
omega = 2 pi / 0.16 = 39 rad s^-1, consistent with about 40 rad s^-1.

questions.question: A toy aeroplane completes 12 revolutions in 6 s. Select the expression giving its angular velocity in rad s^-1.
questions.answer: B: 12 x 2 pi / 6
steps: 12 revolutions in 6 s is 12 / 6 = 2 revolutions per second.
Each revolution is 2 pi rad, so omega = 12 x 2 pi / 6 = 12.6 rad s^-1, which is option B.

questions.question: A laboratory centrifuge rotates at 1500 revolutions per minute. Select the expression giving its angular velocity in radians per second.
steps: 1500 revolutions per minute is 1500 / 60 revolutions per second.
Multiply by 2 pi rad per revolution: omega = 1500 x 2 pi / 60 = 157 rad s^-1, option D.

questions.question: A model aeroplane moves at constant speed v in a horizontal circle of radius r, centre O. Using the velocities at two positions, derive the equation for its centripetal acceleration, with a vector diagram.
questions.answer: a = v^2 / r, directed towards the centre O.
steps: Velocities at the two positions are tangent to the circle and have equal magnitude v.
The vector change in velocity dv = vB - vA points towards the centre O.
For a small angle theta between the positions, dv is approximately v theta, and theta = v dt / r.
a = dv / dt = v^2 / r, directed to the centre.

questions.question: A 1.55 kg model aeroplane moves in a horizontal circle of radius 28.5 m at 22.5 m/s. The lift is vertically upwards and equal to twice its weight. The wire breaks if the tension exceeds 35 N. Deduce whether the wire breaks.
questions.answer: Tension is about 31 N, which is less than 35 N, so the wire does not break.
steps: Lift L = 2 mg = 2 x 1.55 x 9.81 = 30.4 N upwards; weight mg = 15.2 N downwards.
Net vertical force from lift and weight is 15.2 N upwards, so the wire's vertical component must be 15.2 N downwards.
The horizontal component of tension gives the centripetal force: T_h = m v^2 / r = 1.55 x 22.5^2 / 28.5 = 27.5 N.
Total tension T = sqrt(15.2^2 + 27.5^2) = sqrt(989) = 31.5 N.
31 N is less than 35 N, so the wire does not break.

questions.question: A coin of mass 8.8 g on a disk of diameter 30 cm is tilted by raising one edge by 6.3 cm until the coin just starts to slide. Show that the maximum frictional force is about 0.02 N.
questions.answer: Maximum friction f = mg sin(theta) = 0.018 N, which is about 0.02 N.
steps: The disk's diameter of 30 cm is the slope length, so sin(theta) = 6.3 / 30 = 0.21.
Just before sliding, friction acting up the slope balances the component of weight down the slope.
Maximum friction f = m g sin(theta) = 0.0088 x 9.81 x 0.21.
f = 0.018 N, which rounds to about 0.02 N.

questions.question: The disk rotates on a turntable at 45 revolutions per minute. Calculate its angular velocity.
questions.answer: Angular velocity = 4.7 rad s^-1.
steps: Frequency f = 45 rev / 60 s = 0.75 rev s^-1.
omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 0.75.
omega = 4.71 rad s^-1, which is about 4.7 rad s^-1.

questions.question: The maximum friction is 0.02 N and the coin (8.8 g) rotates at 4.7 rad/s on a disk of radius 15 cm. Deduce whether the estimate of 5 cm for the closest the coin can be to the edge without sliding is suitable.
questions.answer: Suitable: the coin can be at most about 10 cm from the centre, so the closest it can be to the edge is about 5 cm.
steps: At the limit, friction supplies the centripetal force: f_max = m omega^2 r.
The coin can be at most about 10 cm from the centre, so it must be at least 15 - 10 = 5 cm from the edge.
The student's estimate of about 5 cm is therefore suitable.

questions.question: The washing machine drum rotates at 1400 revolutions per minute. Show that its angular velocity is about 150 rad s^-1.
questions.answer: omega = 146.6 rad s^-1, which is about 150 rad s^-1.
steps: Frequency f = 1400 / 60 = 23.3 rev s^-1.
omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 23.3 = 146.6 rad s^-1.
This rounds to about 150 rad s^-1, as required.

questions.question: The drum has diameter 45 cm and rotates at 1400 rev/min. Calculate the centripetal acceleration of a point on its circumference.
questions.answer: Centripetal acceleration = 4.8 x 10^3 m s^-2.
steps: Radius r = 45 cm / 2 = 0.225 m.
Angular velocity omega = 146.6 rad s^-1 from part (i).
a = 4.8 x 10^3 m s^-2, directed towards the axis of the drum.

questions.question: Add labelled arrows to each diagram to show the forces acting on the item of clothing in the drum.
questions.answer: Both diagrams: weight mg vertically downwards. Normal contact force N from the drum, directed towards the centre: upwards at the bottom and downwards at the top.
steps: Bottom position: draw the weight mg downwards, and the normal (contact) force N from the drum wall pointing upwards towards the centre; N is longer than mg.
Top position: draw the weight mg downwards, and the normal force N from the drum wall pointing downwards towards the centre.
Label each arrow (weight, normal contact force).

questions.question: The drum rotates at constant speed. Explain how the forces on the item of clothing vary between the bottom and the top of the drum.
questions.answer: The normal force is largest at the bottom (N = m v^2/r + mg) and smallest at the top (N = m v^2/r - mg), while the resultant centripetal force stays constant.
steps: The clothing moves in a vertical circle at constant speed, so the resultant force towards the centre is always m v^2 / r.
At the bottom, the normal force acts upwards and weight downwards: N - mg = m v^2 / r, so N = m v^2 / r + mg.
At the top, the normal force and weight both act downwards towards the centre: N + mg = m v^2 / r, so N = m v^2 / r - mg.
The normal force is greatest at the bottom and least at the top, so the clothing is pressed hardest against the drum at the bottom.

questions.question: Water leaves the drum through the holes as it rotates. Describe the path of the water as it leaves the holes.
questions.answer: The water travels in a straight line, tangent to the circle at the hole it leaves through.
steps: Once the water leaves a hole, no inward force from the drum acts on it.
By Newton's first law, the water continues with the velocity it had at the instant of leaving.
That velocity is tangent to the circular path, so the water moves in a straight line tangent to the drum.

questions.question: Two sources produce waves with a phase difference of 40 degrees. Select the expression that gives this angle in radians.
steps: 360 degrees = 2 pi radians, so 1 degree = 2 pi / 360 rad.
40 degrees = 40 x 2 pi / 360 = 0.70 rad, option A.

questions.question: The turntable is rotated through 160 degrees in 2.2 s. Show that the average angular velocity of the glass is about 1.3 rad s^-1.
questions.answer: omega = 2.79 rad / 2.2 s = 1.27 rad s^-1, which is about 1.3 rad s^-1.
steps: Convert the angle: 160 degrees x pi / 180 = 2.79 rad.
Average angular velocity = angle / time = 2.79 / 2.2 s.
= 1.27 rad s^-1, which rounds to about 1.3 rad s^-1.

questions.question: Explain why the glass has the same angular velocity wherever it is placed on the turntable, but its velocity varies with its position.
questions.answer: All points on the rigid turntable turn through the same angle each second, so omega is the same; the linear speed v = omega r depends on the radius r.
steps: The turntable is a rigid body, so every point turns through the same angle in the same time.
Therefore the angular velocity omega is the same for every position of the glass.
The linear velocity of a point at radius r is v = omega r.
A glass further from the centre has a larger radius and so a larger velocity.

questions.question: The maximum frictional force between the glass and the turntable is given by an expression in m, the mass of the glass. Someone says that a glass placed less than 5 cm from the edge of a 50.0 cm turntable (omega = 1.3 rad/s) will slide. Deduce whether they are correct.
questions.answer: They are correct: the glass starts to slide when closer than about 5.6 cm to the edge, so a glass less than 5 cm from the edge will slide.
steps: The glass stays on the turntable while the friction can provide the centripetal force: m omega^2 x <= m g / 30, where x is the distance from the centre.
x <= g / (30 omega^2) = 9.81 / (30 x 1.3^2) = 0.19 m = 19 cm from the centre.
The turntable radius is 25.0 cm, so the glass slides if it is more than 19.3 cm from the centre, that is closer than 25.0 - 19.3 = 5.6 cm to the edge.

A glass less than 5 cm from the edge is within this range (for example, at 5 cm from the edge x = 20 cm: m omega^2 x = 0.34 m N compared with the maximum friction m g / 30 = 0.33 m N), so the claim is correct.

questions.question: Two identical glasses are placed at the same distance from the edge of the turntable, one full of water and one empty. Explain whether either is more likely to slide as the turntable rotates.
questions.answer: Neither: the required centripetal force and the maximum friction are both proportional to mass, so the mass cancels and both are equally likely to slide.
steps: The centripetal force needed is m omega^2 r, which is proportional to the mass m.
The maximum friction is also proportional to mass, since it depends on the normal force (mg).
Both sides of the comparison scale with mass, so the mass cancels.
The full and empty glasses are therefore equally likely to slide at the same distance from the edge.

questions.question: A model aeroplane moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle, with velocities vF at F and vG at G. Select the correct vector diagram showing the change in velocity from F to G.
questions.answer: C
steps: The change in velocity is delta v = v_G - v_F = v_G + (-v_F).
In diagram C, v_G and -v_F are drawn head to tail, and delta v is the closing side from the start of v_G to the end of -v_F, so delta v = v_G + (-v_F).
A has v_G + delta v = v_F (delta v is the wrong way round), B adds v_F and v_G, and D draws v_F reversed with delta v pointing the wrong way.

questions.question: A propeller sweeps a circle of radius 4.1 cm and pushes air backwards at 2.4 m/s. The density of air is 1.3 kg m^-3. Show that the mass of air pushed back in 0.20 s is about 3 x 10^-3 kg.
questions.answer: m = rho A v t = 1.3 x 5.28 x 10^-3 x 2.4 x 0.20 = 3.3 x 10^-3 kg, which is about 3 x 10^-3 kg.
steps: Area swept by the propeller A = pi r^2 = pi x 0.041^2 = 5.28 x 10^-3 m^2.
Volume of air pushed in time t: V = A v t = 5.28 x 10^-3 x 2.4 x 0.20 = 2.53 x 10^-3 m^3.
This is about 3 x 10^-3 kg, as required.

questions.question: Determine the momentum of the air pushed backwards by the propeller in 0.20 s.
questions.answer: Momentum = 7.9 x 10^-3 kg m s^-1 (N s).
steps: The air is pushed backwards at speed v = 2.4 m s^-1.
The mass of air pushed in 0.20 s is m = 3.3 x 10^-3 kg from part (i).
Momentum p = m v = 3.3 x 10^-3 x 2.4 = 7.9 x 10^-3 kg m s^-1.

questions.question: Determine the forwards force exerted on the aeroplane by the action of the propeller.
questions.answer: Force = 0.040 N (about 4 x 10^-2 N), acting forwards on the aeroplane.
steps: By Newton's third law, the forwards force on the aeroplane equals the rate of change of momentum of the backward-moving air.
F = change in momentum / time = 7.9 x 10^-3 / 0.20 s.
F = 0.040 N, acting forwards on the aeroplane.

questions.question: The forwards and backwards forces on the toy aeroplane are equal in magnitude. Add to the diagram the other forces acting on the toy aeroplane.
questions.answer: Add two forces at the aeroplane: tension T along the thread (up and towards the fixed point) and weight mg vertically downwards.
steps: Draw the tension T in the thread as an arrow along the thread, from the aeroplane up towards the fixed point (at angle theta to the vertical).
Draw the weight mg as an arrow vertically downwards from the aeroplane.
The forward thrust and backward air drag on the aeroplane are equal and opposite, so they cancel and only T and mg give the resultant force towards the centre.

questions.question: Show that the angle theta of the thread to the vertical for the toy aeroplane in a horizontal circle of radius r at speed v is given by tan(theta) = v^2 / (r g). (The target expression is not reproduced in the text extraction.)
questions.answer: tan(theta) = v^2 / (r g), equivalently tan(theta) = omega^2 r / g.
steps: The equal forwards and backwards forces cancel, so the only horizontal force is the horizontal component of tension.
Vertically T cos(theta) = mg, since there is no vertical acceleration.
Horizontally, towards the centre, T sin(theta) = m v^2 / r.
Dividing gives tan(theta) = v^2 / (r g).

questions.question: The thread makes an angle of 22 degrees to the vertical and the radius of the circle is 21 cm. Calculate the time for the toy aeroplane to complete one revolution.
questions.answer: T = 1.4 s for one revolution.
steps: Vertically T_thread cos(theta) = mg and horizontally T_thread sin(theta) = m omega^2 r, so tan(theta) = omega^2 r / g.
Rearrange: omega^2 = g tan(theta) / r, with r = 21 cm = 0.21 m.
Period T = 2 pi / omega = 6.283 / 4.344 = 1.446 s.
So the time for one revolution is 1.4 s (2 s.f.).
